abstract:
We study the question of explicitly constructing variety-evasive subspace families, a pseudorandom primitive introduced by Guo (Computational Complexity 2024) that generalizes both hitting sets and lossless rank condensers. Roughly speaking, a variety-evasive subspace family ℋ is a collection of subspaces such that for every algebraic variety V in a fixed family ℱ, there is some subspace W ∈ ℋ that is in general position with respect to V.
We give an explicit construction of a subspace families that evade all degree-d varieties in an n-dimensional affine or projective space. Our construction improves on the size of the variety-evasive subspace families constructed by Guo and, for varieties of degree n^{1 + Ω(1)}, is polynomially close to Guo’s lower bound on the size of any such variety-evasive subspace family. Our variety-evasive subspace families rely on an improved construction of hitting sets for Chow forms of algebraic varieties.

      Abstract
We study the question of explicitly constructing variety-evasive subspace families, a pseudorandom
primitive introduced by Guo (Computational Complexity 2024) that generalizes both hitting sets
and lossless rank condensers. Roughly speaking, a variety-evasive subspace family H is a collection
of subspaces such that for every algebraic variety V in a fixed family F, there is some subspace
W ∈ H that is in general position with respect to V .
    We give an explicit construction of a subspace families that evade all degree-d varieties in an
n-dimensional affine or projective space. Our construction improves on the size of the variety-evasive
subspace families constructed by Guo and, for varieties of degree n1+Ω(1) , is polynomially close to
Guo’s lower bound on the size of any such variety-evasive subspace family. Our variety-evasive
subspace families rely on an improved construction of hitting sets for Chow forms of algebraic
varieties.

 1      Introduction

1.1     Background
The probabilistic method is a powerful tool with widespread use throughout mathematics.
Many objects of interest throughout combinatorics and computer science, such as Ramsey
graphs and randomness extractors, can be shown to exist via the probabilistic method, often
with excellent parameters. While probabilistic arguments excel at demonstrating existence,
they fall short of providing an efficient, deterministic means of constructing the object of
interest. One of the main goals of pseudorandomness is to obtain explicit constructions
of objects that exhibit properties similar to those enjoyed by a randomly-chosen object.
Not only are explicit constructions interesting in their own right, but they are all the more
important in algorithmic applications such as derandomization, where the aim is to reduce
or eliminate the use of randomness as an algorithmic resource.
    Over time, the theory of pseudorandomness has developed into a rich area of theoretical
computer science that studies a variety of objects, including expander graphs, list-decodable
codes, randomness extractors, pseudorandom generators, and the numerous connections
and relationships between them [14]. More recently, a parallel theory of linear-algebraic
pseudorandomness has also appeared. This theory studies collections of linear maps that

       satisfy various pseudorandom properties, including rank extractors and rank condensers,
       subspace designs, dimension expanders, and subspace-evasive sets, where the dimension of
       vector spaces plays a role analogous to that of min-entropy in classical pseudorandomness.
           In this work, we study the construction of variety-evasive subspace families, a linear-
       algebraic pseudorandom object introduced by Guo [7]. Roughly speaking, a variety-evasive
       subspace family H is a collection of linear or affine spaces such that for any algebraic variety
       V of interest, there is some subspace W ∈ H that is in general position with respect to V .
       For example, if V is a curve in the plane and H is a collection of lines, then there should be
       some line W ∈ H such that the intersection V ∩ W is nonempty and zero-dimensional. More
       generally, when the variety V is fixed, most linear spaces (and in fact, most varieties) W
       will satisfy codim (V ∩ W ) = codim (V ) + codim (W ), and a variety-evasive subspace family
       must contain a subspace W that intersects V in a manner similar to a random subspace.
       This is the sort of behavior captured by the notion of one variety evading another, defined
       below.

       ▶ Definition 1.1 (Evasiveness). Let V and W be irreducible subvarieties of Pn or An . We
       say that W evades V if

          dim(V ∩ W ) ≤ dim(V ) + dim(W ) − n.

       If V and W are affine varieties, we say that W strongly evades V if the above holds with
       equality whenever the right-hand side is nonnegative. If V is a reducible variety, we say that
       W (strongly) evades V if W (strongly) evades each irreducible component of V .

          When V and W are affine varieties, it may be the case that V ∩ W = ∅, even though
       codim (V ) + codim (W ) is not large enough to force this intersection to be empty in general.
       The notion of W strongly evading V adds the constraint that the intersection V ∩ W should
       have the expected codimension of codim (V ) + codim (W ) whenever this is possible.
          As a matter of notational convenience, we also define the notion of a k-subspace family.

       ▶ Definition 1.2 (k-Subspace family). For 0 ≤ k ≤ n, a k-subspace family is a finite collection
       of k-dimensional subspaces of Pn . Similarly, an affine k-subspace family is a finite collection
       of k-dimensional affine subspaces of An .

          We can now define variety-evasive subspace families, the main object of study in this
       work.

       ▶ Definition 1.3 (Variety-evasive subspace families [7]). Let F be a family of subvarieties of
       Pn (or of An ) and let H be a k-subspace (or affine k-subspace) family.
       1. We say that the family H is (strongly) F-evasive if for every V ∈ F, there is some W ∈ H
          that (strongly) evades V . In the case where F is the family of all degree-d subvarieties,
          we say that H is (strongly) (n, d)-evasive.
       2. We say that H is (strongly) (F, ε)-evasive if for every V ∈ F, a randomly-chosen W ∈ H
          (strongly) evades V with probability at least 1 − ε. When F is the family of all degree-d
          subvarieties, we say that H is (strongly) (n, d, ε)-evasive.

           As observed by Guo [7], variety-evasive subspace families are a common generalization
       of two natural problems in algebraic pseudorandomness. The first such problem is the
       construction of hitting sets for arithmetic circuits, a common approach to derandomizing
       algorithms for the polynomial identity testing problem. A hitting set H ⊆ Fn is a collection
       of points such that for every nonzero polynomial f ∈ C in a circuit class C of interest, there
       is some point α ∈ H such that f (α) ̸= 0. The point α witnesses the fact that f is nonzero

as a polynomial. An efficient, deterministic construction of such a hitting set immediately
implies a deterministic algorithm with similar complexity for testing polynomials f ∈ C.
Geometrically, one can view a hitting set as a set of points H such that for every hypersurface
V defined by a polynomial f ∈ C, there is a point α ∈ H such that α ∈     / V . Taking FC to be
the family of hypersurfaces defined by polynomials in C, a hitting set is precisely a FC -evasive
0-subspace family.
    The second task generalized by variety-evasive subspace families is the construction of
lossless rank condensers. Rank condensers, first appearing in the work of Gabizon and
Raz [6], are another of the myriad objects studied in linear-algebraic pseudorandomness.
A lossless rank condenser E ⊆ Fr×n is a collection of linear maps Fn → Fr such that for
every r-dimensional subspace V , there is some map E ∈ E where the image of V under
E remains r-dimensional. Dualizing, this is precisely the same as requiring the kernel of
E to only intersect V at the origin, or equivalently, that the linear spaces in projective
space Pn−1 corresponding to ker E and V have empty intersection. Thus, a lossless rank
condenser is exactly the same object as an (n − r − 1)-subspace family in Pn−1 that evades
all dimension-(r − 1) linear spaces.
    Besides their generalization of other tasks in algebraic pseudorandomness, explicitly
constructing variety-evasive subspace families is a natural task from the point of view of
algebraic geometry. For example, as we will see later, variety-evasive subspace families can
easily be used to construct Noether normalizing maps for algebraic varieties.
    Guo [7] gives the only known construction of variety-evasive subspace families. To
describe his result, we need the following function. For n, d ∈ N and k ∈ {0, 1, . . . , n − 1},

1.2    Our results
We give an improved construction of (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace families. Just like Guo’s
construction, ours is explicit and can be carried out in time polynomial in the size of the
evasive subspace family H (and log p, if F has characteristic p > 0).
▶ Theorem 1.4. Let n, d ∈ N, k ∈ {0, 1, . . . , n − 1}, and 0 < ε < 1. There is an explicit
(n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace family (resp. strongly (n, d, ε)-evasive affine k-subspace family) H
of size poly(((n − k)d + 1)n−k , ε−1 ). Moreover, there is a deterministic algorithm that on
input (n, d, ε) runs in time poly(|H|) and prints defining equations of the subspaces in H.

           To compare our construction with that of Guo, we use the simplified bound from [7,
       Theorem 1.7], which asserts an explicit construction of an (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace family
       of size poly(nmin(k+1,n−k,d)d , d, ε−1 ). In contrast, we construct explicit (n, d, ε)-evasive k-
       subspace families of size poly(((n − k)d + 1)n−k , ε−1 ). This improves the dependence on
       d, which may be exponentially larger than n and k; for example, a variety cut out by n/2
       quadratic equations will generally have degree 2n/2 .
           Guo’s work shows that in order to construct an (n, d)-evasive k-subspace family (and
       similarly an (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace family), it suffices to construct a hitting set for Chow
       forms of equidimensional projective varieties of dimension n − k − 1 (see Definition 3.3 for
       the precise definition). The Chow form of such a variety is a polynomial in n − k sets of n + 1
       variables each, which are thought of as encoding n − k linear equations. The Chow form has
       the remarkable property that it evaluates to zero exactly when these linear equations have
       a solution lying on the variety; equivalently, the Chow form is nonzero exactly when the
       subspace defined by these linear equations evades the variety. If the underlying projective
       variety has degree d, then the Chow form will be a polynomial of degree d in each set of n − k
       variables, for a total degree of (n − k) · d. Using this bound on the degree, Guo [7] bounds
       the sparsity of the Chow form and uses the work of Klivans and Spielman [10] to construct a
       hitting set for Chow forms. To construct (n, d, ε)-evasive subspace families, Guo [7] invokes
       a result of Agrawal, Gurjar, Korwar, and Saxena [1] that provides a stronger guarantee than
       a hitting set: they construct an explicit set of points H such that for all polynomials f of a
       given sparsity bound, a 1 − ε fraction of points in H hit f . Applying this to Chow forms
       results in (n, d, ε)-evasive subspace families.
           Our Theorem 1.4 stems from an improved construction of hitting sets for Chow forms:
       we reduce the number of variables from (n − k)(n + 1) down to n − k while only increasing
       the degree by a factor of n. This allows us to construct (n, d)-evasive k-subspace families
       using hitting sets for polynomials of individual degree dn in n − k variables, resulting in
       the improved parameters of Theorem 1.4. To obtain (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace families, we
       proceed in the same manner as Guo, applying the work of Agrawal, Gurjar, Korwar, and
       Saxena [1] to the variable-reduced Chow form.
           We also give a simple construction of (n, d)-evasive k-subspace families that eliminates
       the polynomial overhead appearing in Theorem 1.4 and does not rely on the notion of Chow
       forms.

       ▶ Theorem 1.5. Let n, d ∈ N and k ∈ {0, 1, . . . , n − 1}. There is an explicit (n, d)-evasive
       k-subspace family (resp. strongly (n, d)-evasive affine k-subspace family) H of size at most
       (nd + 1)n−k . Moreover, there is a deterministic algorithm that receives n, d, and k as input
       and prints the subspace family H in time (nd + 1)O(n−k) .

          As an application of our main result, we give an explicit construction of Noether nor-
       malizing maps. Noether normalization is a useful basic result in commutative algebra. In

affine variety V ⊆ An , there is a surjective finite morphism π : V → Ar . Finite morphisms are
particularly nice maps of algebraic varieties: every subvariety of V is mapped to a subvariety
of Ar , and the preimage π −1 (p) of any point p ∈ Ar will be a finite set.

▶ Corollary 1.6. Let n, d ∈ N, r ∈ {0, 1, . . . , n}, k := n − r − 1, and let ε > 0. There is an
explicit collection L of linear maps An → Ar of size poly(((n − k)d)n−k , ε−1 ) and computable
in time poly(|L|) such that the following hold.
 1. For every projective variety V ⊆ Pn of dimension r − 1 and degree at most d, at least a
    1 − ε fraction of maps π ∈ L induce a surjective finite morphism from V to Pr−1 .
 2. For every affine variety V ⊆ An of dimension r and degree at most d, at least a 1 − ε
    fraction of maps π ∈ L restrict to a surjective finite morphism from V to Pr .

   The proof of Corollary 1.6 is exactly the same as [7, Theorems 1.12 and 1.13], but
using the (n, d, ε)-evasive subspace families of Theorem 1.4 instead of the subspace families
constructed by Guo, so we omit further details.

 2     Preliminaries
Throughout this work, we use F to denote an algebraically closed field. The ring of polynomials
in n + 1 variables is denoted F [x0 , . . . , xn ]. We use bold letters for vectors, whose length
will be clear from context. We use vector notation to denote monomials: given a ∈ Nn+1 ,
we write xa for the monomial xa0 0 · · · xann . We use An and Pn to denote n-dimensional affine
and projective spaces, respectively.

2.1    Algebraic geometry
We assume basic algebraic geometry at the level of [13]. For us, an algebraic variety is a
Zariski-closed subset of An or Pn ; in particular, a variety may be reducible. We adopt the
convention that the degree of a variety is the sum of the degrees of all of its irreducible
components. For this notion of degree, the following inequality holds, which we call Bézout’s
inequality.

▶ Lemma 2.1 (Bézout’s inequality). For any two varieties V and W , we have deg(V ∩ W ) ≤
deg V · deg W .

A proof of the affine version of Lemma 2.1 is given in [9, Theorem 1], while a proof of the
projective version follows immediately from [5, Chapter 2.3].
   We also need the following lemma, which shows that varieties of small degree and
dimension are contained in linear subspaces of small dimension.

▶ Lemma 2.2. For every projective variety V , there exists a linear subspace L of dimension
at most (dim V + 1) · deg V − 1 such that V ⊆ L.

Proof. First, suppose V is irreducible. Let L ⊆ Pn be a minimal linear subspace such that
V ⊆ L. By [8, Corollary 18.12], we can deduce that V has codimension at most deg V − 1
within L. It follows that L has dimension at most dim V + deg V − 1.

       2.2    Variety-evasive subspace families
       In this subsection, we gather some preparatory lemmas for the construction of variety-
       evasive k-subspace families. In particular, we will see that to construct (n, d, ε)-evasive
       k-subspace families, it suffices to construct a k-subspace family that evades degree-d varieties
       of dimension n − k − 1, and that we may further assume these varieties live in an ambient
       space of dimension (n − k − 1)d. In addition to this, we will see that an (n, d, ε)-evasive
       k-subspace family automatically yields an (n, d, ε′ )-evasive affine k-subspace family with only
       a mild loss in ε′ .
           We first cite a lemma of Guo [7] that shows constructing an (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace
       family reduces to the task of constructing a k-subspace that ε-evades equidimensional
       subvarieties of dimension n − k − 1 and degree d.

       ▶ Lemma 2.3 ([7, Lemma 3.1]). Let F be the family of equidimensional projective subvarieties
       of Pn of dimension n − k − 1 and degree at most d. Suppose H is an (F, ε)-evasive k-subspace
       family. Then H is (n, d, ε)-evasive.

          Next, we show that the dimension of the ambient space can be reduced. As a conse-
       quence of Lemma 2.2, it suffices to construct variety-evasive subspace families when the
       ambient dimension n is at most deg V · dim V . Essentially the same reduction is used in the
       constructions of Guo [7]. We give a proof for completeness.

▶ Lemma 2.5. Let H be an (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace family. Let H′ ⊆ H be the subfamily

in Pn . All except ε |H| elements in H′ evade V . Therefore, H∞ is a (n − 1, d, ε′ )-evasive
subspace family.

       affine varieties. Let V ⊆ An be an affine variety of degree d. Identifying An with the affine
       chart, we can consider V ⊆ Pn . Let V be the projective closure of V , and let V∞ denote
       V ∩ V (x0 ). Both V and V∞ have degree at most d.
           Suppose H ∈ H′ is such that H evades V and H ∩ V (x0 ) evades V∞ . Let W be an
       irreducible component of V , let W be the projective closure of W , and let W∞ denote
       W ∩ V (x0 ). By assumption, every component of W ∩ H has dimension dim W + k − n. If
       dim W + k − n < 0, then this intersection is empty. In this case, W ∩ H ∩ An is also empty,
       and therefore H ∩ An evades W . Otherwise, we have dim W + k − n ≥ 0.
           To show that H ∩ An evades W , it suffices to show that W ∩ H ̸⊆ V (x0 ). This will
       guarantee that W ∩H ∩An is nonempty and has the correct dimension. To this end, note that
       dim W∞ = dim W − 1. Since H ∩ V (x0 ) evades W∞ , every component of W ∩ H ∩ V (x0 ) has
       dimension dim W + k − n − 1. Since every component of W ∩ H has dimension dim W + k − n,
       no component of W ∩ H lies completely in the hyperplane at infinity, completing the proof
       that H ∩ An evades W . Since this holds for every component W of V , we deduce that H ∩ An
       evades V .

       of hyperplanes in H′ such that either H does not evade V or such that H ∩ V (x0 ) does not
       evade V∞ is at most 2ε′ . Therefore, the restriction of H′ to the affine chart is a strongly
       (n, d, 2ε′ )-evasive affine k-subspace family.                                                    ◀


        3     Construction of variety-evasive subspace families
       We give two constructions of variety-evasive subspace families. The first is a simple con-
       struction meant to illustrate our main technical observation. The second is a more involved
       construction that allows us to obtain improved epsilon variety-evasive subspace families.

       3.1    Basic construction
       Let V ⊆ Pn be an projective variety of dimension r. The intersection of V with a general
       hyperplane is a variety of dimension r − 1. Typically, to obtain an effective version of this
       fact, one picks a point on each irreducible component of V and controls the probability that a
       randomly-chosen hyperplane H does not pass through the chosen points. If H does not pass
       through these points, then H properly intersects each component of V , so the intersection
       V ∩ H will have dimension exactly r − 1.
            We implement this argument in the following lemma. Here, the coefficients of the
       hyperplane H are not picked independently, but are instead chosen from points of the form
       (1, γ, γ 2 , . . . , γ n ) for γ ∈ F. When we invoke this lemma in the proof of Theorem 1.5, we will
       need to choose a hyperplane H that properly intersects a collection of irreducible varieties
       that need not be the irreducible components of a single variety. For example, one variety in
       the given collection may be properly contained in another.

    Applying Lemma 3.1 to the irreducible components of a projective variety allows us to
construct a set H of nd + 1 hyperplanes such that for any projective variety V ⊆ Pn of

k-subspace family. We remark that this solves [7, Open Problem 7], which asked for an
explicit construction of a polynomial-size (n, d)-evasive k-subspace family when n − k = O(1).

        tively, intersecting n − k hyperplanes one at a time. To improve this to a construction of an
        (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace family, one natural approach is to ensure that at each step, the
        probability of picking a hyperplane that does not properly intersect a variety V is bounded

    In the notation of Corollary 3.4, the polynomial ϕ(CV ) is a nonzero polynomial of
individual degree nd in r + 1 variables with the property that the subspace defined by the
linear forms with coefficients γ 0 , . . . , γ r evades V if ϕ(CV )(γ 0 , . . . , γ r ) ̸= 0. The construction
of Theorem 1.5 can be thought of as a construction of a hitting set for the restricted Chow
form ϕ(CV ). To obtain (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace families, we instead apply an ε-hitting set
to the restricted Chow form ϕ(CV ). An ε-hitting set has exactly the guarantee we need: it is a
finite set H such that a 1−ε fraction of points (γ 0 , . . . , γ r ) ∈ H satisfy ϕ(CV )(γ 0 , . . . , γ r ) ̸= 0.
We make this observation precise in the following corollary.
▶ Corollary 3.5. Suppose P is an ε-hitting set for polynomials of individual degree nd in
n − k variables. Then there exists a (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace family H of size at most |P|.
Moreover, there is a deterministic algorithm that takes P as input, prints the set H, and
runs in time poly(n, |P|).
Proof. The evasive family of subspaces is constructed as follows. For each point µ ∈ P, let
Hµ be the linear subspace defined by the linear forms x0 + µi x1 + · · · + µni xn for i ∈ [n − k].
Let H′ be the resulting family of subspaces.
    Let V be an arbitrary equidimensional variety of dimension n − k − 1 and degree d, and
let CV be its Chow form. Let ϕ be the map defined in Corollary 3.4, so ϕ(CV ) is a nonzero
polynomial of individual degree nd in n − k variables. Since P is a ε-hitting set for such
polynomials, for all except ε |P| elements in P, we have ϕ(CV )(µ) ̸= 0. Therefore, for all
except ε |H′ | of the subspaces H ∈ H′ , we have V ∩ H = ∅.
    Note that the exceptional set of ε |H′ | vector spaces H ∈ H′ such that V ∩ H = ̸ ∅ contains
all those subspaces in H′ that are not k-dimensional. Therefore, if we define H to be the set
of k-dimensional subspaces in H′ , then all except ε |H| elements in H evade V . Since V was
an arbitrary equidimensional variety of dimension n − k − 1 and degree d, we can invoke
Lemma 2.3 to deduce that H is (n, d, ε)-evasive.
    It is clear that the set H′ can be obtained in polynomial time from the ε-hitting set P.
To prune H′ to the (n, d, ε)-evasive k-subspace family H, we need to remove from H′ those
subspaces that are not k-dimensional. This is a basic linear algebra calculation that can be
performed in poly(n) time for each element of H′ .                                             ◀

of Agrawal, Gurjar, Korwar, and Saxena [1], as instantiated by Guo [7]. The version we state
here is adapted to polynomials of bounded individual degree instead of bounded total degree,
but follows exactly the same proof as [7, Lemma 2.3].
▶ Lemma 3.6 ([7, Lemma 2.3], [1, Lemma 4]). For every d, n ∈ N and ε ∈ (0, 1), there exists
an ε-hitting set P for the set of all polynomials of individual degree d in n variables. The set
P has size and bit complexity poly (d + 1)n , ε−1 and can be constructed in time poly(|P|).

construction of (n, d, ε)-evasive subspaces.
